title: The Log Is The Agent - Ishaan Sehgal, Omnara

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's core thesis is that an agent's identity and architecture should center on a durable append-only log with a disposable execution loop and everything else as projections. Omnara builds developer infrastructure for managed agents, and the log-first architectural thesis applies broadly across all agent systems. The talk covers architectural design of log-first agents and production reliability concerns including crash recovery, scalability, and provider migration. Accessible analogies like Skyrim save files and database logs make architectural concepts approachable for a technical audience. A conference presentation at AI Engineer using analogies, architectural models, and a platform announcement. summary: Ishaan Sehgal, CEO of Omnara, presents the thesis that an AI agent's identity is its log, not the model, runtime, or tools. He opens with a video game analogy: a Skyrim character is the save file, not the game engine, console, or controller. If the PlayStation breaks, the character persists because identity lives in the data. Similarly, an agent's identity, history, and state live in its append-only event log—every user input, model output, tool call, result, permission, and failure. The log is the primary primitive; everything else (model context, UI, debugging, auditing, compaction) is a projection over it. The execution loop is disposable: a worker reads the log, advances one step, writes the result, and disappears. Any worker can resume later. The executor calls the model provider, writes results to the log, dispatches tools to execution environments, and appends tool results back; a different worker then reconstructs state and continues. This is essential for real-world survival: workers crash, machines restart, sandboxes disappear, tool calls time out, providers fail, users disconnect. If an agent is a running process, these failures are terrifying; if the agent is the log, they are merely execution details. This mirrors how databases work—tables and indexes are projections over a durable underlying log. He addresses two objections. Compaction: context windows are finite, so logs must be compacted, but compaction is lossy and is just one projection; the full log remains canonical. External state: tools modify files, send emails, create issues—state outside the log. The log stores the agent's view of the world, not the entire world. Treating the log as primitive yields structural properties: reliability, scalability, forkability, multiplayer, migration, ownership. Current infrastructure treats logs as fragile afterthoughts—Claude Code and Codex write messy JSONL, OpenCode uses SQLite with corruption issues. The deepest lock-in is log ownership: if a provider owns your log, they own your agent. Anthropic and Google are building managed agents that aim to own hosted loops, memory, and compaction. Omnara is debuting an open-source managed agents platform built entirely around the session log, ensuring users fully own, inspect, and control their logs. Sehgal closes by urging the audience to stop treating the log as system exhaust and start treating it as the system itself.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Video Game Analogy
sections.summary: Ishaan introduces the thesis using a Skyrim analogy: a game character is the save file, not the engine, console, or controller. If hardware dies, the character persists because identity lives in the data. He applies this framing to agents: the agent is its log, not the model or runtime.

sections.title: The Log as Primitive and Disposable Loop
sections.summary: Defines the log as append-only event history of every state transition. The model reads the log and proposes next action; the tool runner executes and appends results. The loop is disposable—any worker can claim a session, advance one step, write the result, and disappear.

sections.title: Database Analogy and Projections
sections.summary: Draws parallel to databases: underneath tables and indexes is a durable log, and everything else is a view. Agents need the same inversion—context, UI, debugging, auditing, and compaction are all projections over the log, but the log itself is the durable history.

sections.title: Two Objections: Compaction and External State
sections.summary: Addresses compaction: context windows are finite so logs must be compacted, but compaction is lossy and is just one projection. The full log is the record. Addresses external state: tools change state outside the log (files, emails, issues), but the log stores the agent's view of the world, not the entire world, like a Skyrim save file.

sections.title: System Properties from Log-First Architecture
sections.summary: Reliability: agents survive process death. Scalability: one process advances thousands of agents. Forkability: branch logs across different models. Multiplayer: sharing means granting log access. Migration: moving providers becomes an adapter problem, not an identity problem.

sections.title: Current Infrastructure Critique and Ownership/Lock-in
sections.summary: Critiques current tools: Claude Code and Codex write fragile JSONL, OpenCode uses SQLite with corruption issues. The deepest lock-in is log ownership—if a provider owns your log, they own your agent. Anthropic and Google are building managed agents to own hosted loops. Omnara's architecture centers the log as the primary primitive.

sections.title: Real-World Failure Handling and Closing
sections.summary: Describes the full executor cycle: call model, write to log, dispatch tools to execution environments, append results, and a different worker reconstructs state to continue. This is essential because workers crash, machines restart, sandboxes disappear, tool calls time out, and providers fail. If an agent is a running process, these failures are terrifying; if the agent is the log, they are execution details. Introduces Omnara's open-source managed agents platform built around the session log with full user ownership, inspection, and control. Closes by urging the audience to stop treating the log as system exhaust and treat it as the system itself.
